ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The common peroneal nerve branches from the sciatic nerve, winds around the fibular head, and supplies dorsiflexion and eversion. Clinically, its injury causes foot drop and sensory loss over the lateral shin. Recognising its course helps avoid iatrogenic damage and diagnose neuropathies.

sections.p: The common peroneal nerve is the lateral division of the sciatic nerve, emerging at the popliteal fossa and wrapping around the fibular head before splitting into superficial and deep branches.
It runs medially to laterally in the popliteal fossa, then courses laterally along the fibular head, passing between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius.
Superficial to the common peroneal are the small saphenous vein and superficial veins; deep are the popliteal artery and vein, tibial nerve, and lymph nodes.
The nerve receives arterial input from the genicular branches of the popliteal artery and small perforators from the fibular artery.
It gives rise to the deep peroneal nerve (motor to tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, etc.) and superficial peroneal nerve (motor to peroneus longus/ brevis, sensory to lateral foot).
Motor: dorsiflexion of ankle and toes, eversion of foot. Sensory: lateral lower leg and dorsum of foot.
Compression at the fibular head (e.g., from casts, prolonged squatting) or trauma can cause foot drop. In low‑resource settings, prolonged immobilisation or barefoot walking may predispose.
b: Foot drop is a red flag

t.b: Assess dorsiflexion and eversion; loss indicates common peroneal involvement

sections.p: Remember the nerve is superficial at the fibular head; a tight cast or prolonged squatting can compress it. Foot drop is the hallmark sign.
